range-and-counting.label: Range and Counting Patterns
range-and-counting.summary: Use `range(stop)`, `range(start, stop)`, and `range(start, stop, step)` to generate controlled numeric sequences for `for` loops.

sc-range-five-values.title: What does range(5) produce?
sc-range-five-values.prompt: Which list matches the values from `range(5)` in a `for` loop?

help.hint_2: The last value is 4 because the stop boundary 5 is excluded.

sc-range-start-stop.title: Which loop prints 1 to 5?
sc-range-start-stop.prompt: Choose the loop that prints the numbers `1` through `5`, each on its own line.
sc-range-start-stop.hint: To include 5, choose a stop boundary just after it.

help.hint_2: A stop value of 6 leaves 5 as the last produced value.

mc-true-about-range.title: Facts about range()
mc-true-about-range.prompt: Choose all true statements about Python `range()`.
mc-true-about-range.hint: Check the defaults and remember that the stop value is excluded.

help.concept: `range()` supports stop, start/stop, and start/stop/step forms.
help.hint_1: `range(5)` uses a default start of 0 and step of 1.
help.hint_2: A third argument changes the step size.

options.b: The stop value is included in the loop.
options.d: `range()` can help control how many times a loop runs.

mc-even-loop-options.title: Ranges that produce the same even sequence
mc-even-loop-options.prompt: Which loops print exactly `0, 2, 4, 6, 8`, one value per line? Choose all correct answers.
mc-even-loop-options.hint: Because the stop value is excluded, more than one nearby stop boundary can produce the same final value.

help.concept: A step of 2 produces the even pattern; the stop boundary determines whether another value is reached.
help.hint_2: `range(0, 9, 2)` also stops after producing 8 because the next value would be 10.

dr-build-basic-range-loop.title: Build a range(stop) loop
dr-build-basic-range-loop.prompt: Arrange the lines to make valid Python that prints `0` through `4`.
dr-build-basic-range-loop.hint: The print statement belongs inside the `for` block.

help.concept: A `for` header is followed by an indented loop body.

dr-build-step-range.title: Build a stepped range loop
dr-build-step-range.prompt: Arrange the lines to make valid Python that prints even numbers below 10.
dr-build-step-range.hint: Use a step of 2 and indent the print statement.

help.concept: `range(0, 10, 2)` produces the values and the indented loop body prints each one.
help.hint_2: The print line belongs inside the loop.

fb-stop-not-included.title: Complete the stop value idea
fb-stop-not-included.prompt: Fill in the missing word to complete the rule about `range()`.
fb-stop-not-included.hint: The stop value marks the boundary but is not produced.

help.concept: Python ranges exclude their stop value.

fb-stop-not-included.template: In `range(start, stop)`, the stop value is [blank1].

fb-step-even-pattern.title: Complete the step value
fb-step-even-pattern.prompt: Fill in the missing value so the loop counts by twos.

help.concept: The third argument is the amount added between produced values.

ci-print-zero-to-four.title: Use range(stop) with an input boundary
ci-print-zero-to-four.prompt: Read an integer `stop`. Use `for n in range(stop)` to print every value produced by the range, one per line.
ci-print-zero-to-four.hint: With one argument, `range(stop)` starts at 0 and excludes `stop`.

help.concept: The input becomes the exclusive stop boundary.
help.hint_2: Print the loop variable inside the `for` block.

ci-print-zero-to-four.starterCode:
stop = int(input())
# Print the values from range(stop)

0.message: Use `for n in range(stop):` and print `n` inside the loop.

ci-print-one-to-five.title: Use explicit start and stop values
ci-print-one-to-five.prompt: Read integers `start` and `stop`. Use `range(start, stop)` to print every generated value, one per line.

help.concept: Two arguments choose the inclusive start and exclusive stop boundaries.

ci-print-one-to-five.starterCode:
start = int(input())
stop = int(input())
# Print range(start, stop)
ci-print-one-to-five.solutionCode:
start = int(input())
stop = int(input())
for n in range(start, stop):
    print(n)

0.message: Use `for n in range(start, stop):` with both input boundaries.

ci-even-under-ten.title: Use a step to count by twos
ci-even-under-ten.prompt: Read an integer `stop`. Use `range(0, stop, 2)` to print the nonnegative even values below `stop`.
ci-even-under-ten.hint: Start at 0 and use a step of 2.

help.concept: The third range argument controls the jump between generated values.
help.hint_1: The stop boundary is still excluded.

ci-even-under-ten.starterCode:
stop = int(input())
# Print nonnegative even values below stop

0.message: Use `range(0, stop, 2)` so the loop advances by two.

ci-countdown-three-to-one.title: Count backward with a negative step
ci-countdown-three-to-one.prompt: Read an integer `start`. Use `range(start, 0, -1)` to print a countdown from `start` through 1. If `start` is 0, print nothing.
ci-countdown-three-to-one.hint: A negative step moves the generated values downward.

help.concept: For a countdown through 1, use an exclusive stop of 0 and a step of -1.

ci-countdown-three-to-one.starterCode:
start = int(input())
# Count down from start through 1

0.message: Use `range(start, 0, -1)` for a countdown that ends at 1.

ci-print-squares-one-to-four.title: Transform each value from a range
ci-print-squares-one-to-four.prompt: Read an integer `n`. Use `range(1, n + 1)` to print the square of each integer from 1 through `n`. If `n` is 0, print nothing.
ci-print-squares-one-to-four.hint: Use `n + 1` as the exclusive stop so the value `n` is included.

help.concept: A loop can transform each generated range value independently without accumulating a running total.
help.hint_2: Print `value * value` for each generated value.

ci-print-squares-one-to-four.starterCode:
n = int(input())
# Print the squares from 1 through n

0.message: Use `range(1, n + 1)` and print the square of each loop value.

sk-range-basics.title: Start at 0 with range(stop)
sk-range-basics.bodyMarkdown:
A `for` loop can take its values from `range()`.

```python
for n in range(5):
    print(n)
```

`range(5)` produces:

```text
0
1
2
3
4
```

With one argument, `range(stop)`:

- starts at `0`;
- increases by `1`;
- stops **before** `stop`.

So `5` is the boundary, not a value produced by the range.

A useful rule is:

```text
range(stop) -> 0 through stop - 1
```

sk-range-start-stop.title: Choose both start and stop
sk-range-start-stop.bodyMarkdown:
Use two arguments when the sequence should begin somewhere other than `0`.

```python
for n in range(2, 6):
    print(n)
```

The output is:

```text
2
3
4
5
```

With `range(start, stop)`:

- `start` is included;
- `stop` is excluded;
- the default step is still `1`.

That means `range(1, 6)` produces `1` through `5`, while `range(3, 3)` produces no values because the starting point has already reached the stopping boundary.

sk-range-step-patterns.title: Control the jump with a step
sk-range-step-patterns.bodyMarkdown:
A third argument controls how much the value changes each time.

```python
for n in range(0, 10, 2):
    print(n)
```

The output is:

```text
0
2
4
6
8
```

Here the range means:

- start at `0`;
- stop before `10`;
- add `2` each time.

A negative step counts downward:

```python
for n in range(3, 0, -1):
    print(n)
```

This produces:

```text
3
2
1
```

The stop value is excluded in either direction. With a negative step, choose a stop value just below the last value you want to produce.
